extracted.intended_audience: OMB staff, congressional policymakers, regulatory analysts, and regulators preparing regulatory accounting
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating and improving OMB’s annual Draft Report to Congress on the costs and benefits of federal regulations, including recommended standards for coverage, transparency, validation, and presentation of regulatory cost-benefit estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comprehensive coverage of regulations
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB’s totals should not be based on only a small fraction of federal regulation (the Draft Report’s estimates are based on agency estimates for eleven regulations—less than 0.3 percent of final rules published during the year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not restrict reporting to a tiny subset of rules; expand coverage beyond the small set of regulations for which agencies happen to report both costs and benefits so the totals better reflect actual regulatory activity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not limit totals to rules with both cost and benefit estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB should not limit its totals to rules for which agencies estimate both costs and benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report costs even when agencies do not (yet) quantify benefits; provide Congress a review of other reliable estimates of regulatory impacts rather than excluding such rules from aggregate totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include rules classified as 'transfers' and estimate associated deadweight loss
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules that effect transfers (which OMB often treats as mere redistribution) impose real costs such as deadweight loss or excess burden and should not be excluded from totals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Estimate the deadweight loss associated with transfers (e.g., OMB’s excess burden of taxation proxy of 25 percent of revenues is a reference point). Investigate rent-seeking and dissipation of benefits that may turn apparent transfers into real resource costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include regulations with continuing multi-year costs (avoid arbitrary 10-year truncation)
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB’s ten-year rolling aggregation drops regulations first imposed 11 years ago even where they continue to impose significant costs (e.g., DOT drug/alcohol testing, EPA land disposal restrictions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid arbitrary truncation of 'total' costs; when a rule imposes ongoing costs, those continuing costs should be represented rather than removed solely due to age.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include independent agency regulations in aggregate estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulations issued by independent agencies are excluded from OMB’s totals despite producing cost and (sometimes) benefit estimates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although OMB may have less oversight, its congressional mandate does not direct exclusion of independent agencies; OMB should include available independent-agency cost/benefit data in the annual estimates or otherwise account for them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide independent assessment and verification of agency estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: The report currently compiles agency estimates without independent verification; OMB offers no independent assessment of quality or usefulness of agency analyses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OMB should add independent review of agency analyses (at minimum a 'report card' highlighting strengths and weaknesses) to provide assurance that assumptions and methods are reliable and comparable across agencies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency about assumptions and methodologies
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB’s report should provide more detailed information about the assumptions underlying the benefit and cost estimates of individual regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the methods, baselines, valuation approaches, and key modeling assumptions used by agencies so researchers and policymakers can assess comparability and credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present data by regulation and by year (tabular breakdown)
rubrics_metrics.description: A table that reports data by regulation and by year is needed to allow researchers to understand the composition of estimates and how OMB constructed its aggregates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alongside graphical displays, provide a regulation-by-regulation, year-by-year table (including which rules were included/excluded and why) so users can audit and disaggregate totals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make ex post (retrospective) analysis standard for validation
rubrics_metrics.description: Compare post-regulation outcomes to pre-regulation (ex ante) estimates to 'validate' the accuracy of forecasts; retrospective analyses have proved illuminating (e.g., NHTSA center high-mounted stop lamp RIA over/under-estimates).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make ex post evaluation a routine part of regulatory accounting to identify systematic biases, improve future RIAs, and inform elimination/modification of ineffective rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Track costs separately and systematically (analogous to budgetary tracking)
rubrics_metrics.description: Understanding the costs of regulations has value independent of quantified benefits; policymakers track on-budget expenditures and should similarly track regulatory costs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a systematic accounting of regulatory expenditures (cost side) even when benefits are hard to quantify; this supports accountability and informed decision-making.

rubrics_metrics.name: Review and incorporate external literature and alternative estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB should provide a review of available literature (e.g., SBA, Mercatus studies) to give Congress a more comprehensive picture and cross-check OMB’s regulation-by-regulation approach.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summarize findings from independent studies and alternative methodologies as supplementary points of reference; do not rely solely on agency-submitted estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge and address uncertainty in benefit estimates (especially health/mortality valuations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Benefits reported (e.g., EPA particulate matter mortality valuations) are subject to considerable uncertainty, both in magnitude and valuation (monetary value of reducing mortality risk).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly quantify uncertainty ranges, sensitivity analyses, and discuss the statistical and methodological bases for valuations; avoid uncritical reliance on single best-case agency estimates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow Circular A-4 and require identification of market failure before regulating
rubrics_metrics.description: Government decisions based on benefit-cost analysis should begin by identifying whether a systemic market problem exists; Circular A-4 provides guidance on developing and evaluating regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before undertaking regulation, require agencies to demonstrate the market failure the regulation addresses; use Circular A-4 principles in ex ante analyses to improve relevance and quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize dominance of particular estimates and perform sensitivity analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB’s totals are heavily dominated by uncertain EPA estimates (e.g., a single pollutant’s valuation comprises the majority of reported benefits).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify when totals are driven by a few estimates, disclose this dominance, and perform sensitivity analyses to show how aggregates change under alternative plausible assumptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure consistency of methods and assumptions across programs
rubrics_metrics.description: The report currently compiles varied agency methods without assurance that assumptions and methods are consistent across programs and activities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where feasible, standardize or at least document comparable methodological frameworks and assumptions so aggregated figures are meaningful; flag major methodological differences when aggregation is performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for behavioral responses and baseline selection in analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: Prospective RIAs may fail to anticipate behavioral responses (e.g., auto manufacturers’ estimates being more accurate than regulators’) and the proper counterfactual baseline remains a challenge in both ex ante and ex post work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model and discuss likely behavioral changes induced by regulation and carefully justify baseline choices; where behavior is important, treat ex ante estimates with caution and prioritize empirical validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Present net benefits while separately presenting costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Net benefits (benefits minus costs) are theoretically superior as a measure, but there is considerable value in separately examining the cost side.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Report both net benefit calculations and separate cost accounting so policymakers can see both the overall value and the fiscal/resource burdens analogous to budgetary tracking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide a 'report card' on the quality of individual regulatory analyses
rubrics_metrics.description: OMB analysts identify strengths and weaknesses when reviewing significant regulations; those observations should be included in the report in the form of a 'report card' for each analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concise, standardized assessments of each regulation’s RIA quality (methodology, assumptions, data quality, treatment of uncertainty) to add value beyond simple compilation of agency numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use graphical representation but accompany with disaggregated data and documentation
rubrics_metrics.description: Graphs (e.g., Figures 2-1 through 2-3 showing yearly activity and the 'midnight regulation effect') are useful, but must be backed by disaggregated data and methodological documentation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Supply underlying datasets and methodological notes that produce the graphs so researchers can replicate, interrogate, and extend the visualized findings.
